items.title: David Brinkley Interview, 1962-01-10
items.q: Harry Sujan, a local attorney, helped to start the jazz club, which now has a thousand members.

ctx.x: People in New Orleans accept this music on a different social basis than people do all over the world. All over, it's accepted as a form of American culture. In New Orleans, it's a form of music that grew out of a red light district. It's music that people still associate with the problems here.

The New Orleans Jazz Club also is trying to keep the old-time music alive. And here in Beauregard Square, it is about to dedicate its jazz museum, opened last November. The tap dancers are called Cork Chop and Kidney Stoop. Harry Sujan, a local attorney, helped to start the jazz club, which now has a thousand members.

Back in 1947, there just wasn't any jazz here. The only way you could hear it was to play your old 78 records. So that's what we did, until we got brave enough to have our own little concert. Then we started from there.
